title: The First-Time Renter’s Guide: Surviving Your First Month
seoTitle: First-Time Renter Guide: Your First Month
description: You have the keys — now what? Move-in day in order, the first week of utilities and admin, what to buy in week one, and how to get your deposit back.
excerpt: Most renting advice stops at the signature. This one keeps going: move-in day in order, the first week of utility and society admin, what an empty Indian flat actually needs, and the habits that get your deposit back eleven months later.

faq.q: What should I do on the day I get the keys?
faq.a: In this order: photograph every room while the flat is still empty, note and photograph the electricity, water and gas meter readings, count how many keys exist and who else has one, and do an inventory walk with the owner listing everything being left behind and its condition. Send the photos and readings to the owner the same day so there is a shared, timestamped record. It takes about forty minutes and it is the best protection your deposit will ever get.

faq.q: What does "unfurnished" actually include in India?
faq.a: Usually just the walls, floor, doors, windows, kitchen platform, sink and bathroom fittings. It commonly does not include ceiling fans, light fittings or bulbs, a geyser, wardrobes, curtain rods, an exhaust fan or a chimney. "Semi-furnished" has no fixed meaning at all, so ask for a written item-by-item list and get it into the agreement rather than assuming.

faq.q: Does the electricity connection have to be transferred into my name?
faq.a: It depends. Some owners transfer it, others keep the account in their own name and have the tenant reimburse the bill, and what is possible depends on your state distribution company’s rules. Procedures, documents and timelines vary by provider, so check with your own discom directly rather than relying on a general description. Either way, take a meter reading on move-in day and write down the consumer number and billing cycle.

faq.q: What should I buy in the first week, and what can wait?
faq.a: Week one: bulbs and tube lights, fans if there are none, a mattress, curtains even temporary ones, a gas connection and stove, a basic cleaning kit, a few essential kitchen items, and a fridge if you cook. It can wait: proper light fittings, air conditioning, a washing machine, storage furniture and anything decorative. A few weeks of living there will change what you buy, so resist furnishing it all at once.

faq.q: How do I make sure I get my security deposit back?
faq.a: Most of it happens before you ask. Photograph the flat on the day you move in, pay rent traceably so arrears are never in dispute, report problems in writing and early rather than letting them worsen, fix small things yourself, and never make permanent changes without written permission. On the way out, clean properly, take final photos and meter readings with the owner present, and agree the return amount in writing before handing over the keys.

faq.q: Should I pay rent in cash?
faq.a: Avoid it. A bank transfer, UPI payment or cheque leaves a dated record with a name attached, which settles almost any later disagreement in one message. If cash is genuinely unavoidable, insist on a signed receipt every single time with the month clearly written on it, and keep all of them together with your agreement and deposit receipt.

body:
The lights. Nobody warns you about the lights.

Rohit collected the keys at about five on a Saturday evening, stood in the middle of the first flat that was properly his, and thought it was the best-looking empty room he had ever seen. Then the sun went down. There were bulb holders in every ceiling — bare, plastic, hanging there like unfinished sentences — and not one bulb in any of them. No tube lights. No fans either, just hooks and a curl of wire. The bathroom had a geyser point, a socket, and nothing plugged into it.

He ate off a delivery box on the floor with his phone torch propped against the wall, working out which shop nearby was still open at nine at night. That is the first night in an unfurnished Indian flat, and almost everybody gets a version of it once.

None of it was a disaster. It was an order-of-operations problem. Nobody had told him what to do first, second and third. So that is what this is: what to sort before you sign, what to do the day the keys change hands, what week one actually looks like, and how to be the kind of tenant who gets the whole deposit back at the end.

## Nobody hands you the manual

The mental shift is bigger than the logistics, and it lands about four days in.

Up to now, somebody else absorbed the small stuff. A parent, a warden, a hostel office, a landlord who lived downstairs. Something leaked and a person appeared. The bill arrived and then disappeared. You did not know when the water came, because the water simply came.

Now it is you. Not in a frightening way — in a *nobody else is going to notice* way. If the flush runs all night, it runs all night until you deal with it. If the electricity account is still in the previous tenant's name, that stays true until you make it untrue.

The good news is that nearly all of this is one-time work. A first month that feels relentless becomes a home that runs itself in the background. The trick is doing things in the right order, and writing down what you did.

> One rule will save you more money than anything else in this article: everything important goes in writing, and everything you pay leaves a trail. Not because you expect a fight — because memory is a terrible witness eleven months later.

## Before you sign: what "unfurnished" really means here

Briefly, because this deserves its own reading and already has it.

In most Indian cities, *unfurnished* means walls, floor, doors, windows, a kitchen platform, a sink and the bathroom fittings. That is often the entire list. It does not reliably include wardrobes. It very often does not include a geyser, ceiling fans, light fittings, curtain rods, a chimney or exhaust fan, a modular kitchen, or anything to keep food cold.

*Semi-furnished* means whatever the owner has decided it means. Ask for the specific list, item by item, and get it into the agreement. "Semi-furnished" in an advert and "semi-furnished" in the flat are two different objects.

Two things follow. First, the setup cost is real and it is front-loaded — fans, lights, a geyser, curtains and some form of storage all land in the same fortnight as your deposit and your first month's rent. Work that number out before you commit, not after; the [hidden costs of renting in India](/blog/hidden-costs-of-renting-in-india) piece walks through the whole arithmetic, including brokerage, maintenance and move-in charges.

Second, this is exactly what a viewing is for. Open cupboards. Look up at ceilings. Count sockets. The [house-hunting checklist](/blog/house-hunting-checklist-india) and the [questions to ask before renting](/blog/questions-to-ask-before-renting) cover that ground properly. Read them before your first viewing, not after your third.

And read the agreement in advance rather than at the door with a pen in your hand — [rental agreements in India](/blog/rental-agreements-in-india) explains what those clauses actually do to you.

## Move-in day, in order

Do these in sequence, before a single carton crosses the threshold. The whole thing takes about forty minutes, and it is the highest-value forty minutes of your entire tenancy.

**1. Photograph the empty flat.** Every room, every wall, floor to ceiling. Then the specifics: bathroom tiles, under the sink, the kitchen platform, window grilles, the inside of any wardrobe, existing cracks, existing stains, that patch of damp behind the door. Photograph the switchboards.

Do it *before* the boxes arrive, because an empty room photographs honestly and a room with your sofa in it does not. A video helps too — one slow walk-through, narrating what you see. Your phone stamps date and time on all of it, which is the point. Email the set to yourself so a second copy exists with a timestamp you did not control.

**2. Read the meters and photograph them.** Electricity, water if there is a separate meter, gas if it is piped. Get the reading and the meter serial number in the same frame. Send those photos to the owner the same day, with the reading typed out as text. That message is your baseline, and it means a bill covering the previous occupant's April is never your problem.

**3. Count the keys.** How many main-door keys exist? Who else has one? Is there a duplicate with the watchman, the previous tenant, the owner's brother, someone who used to clean the place? Ask plainly. If the answer is vague, a new lock cylinder is cheap — discuss it with the owner rather than doing it quietly.

Collect the rest too: letterbox key, terrace or utility door key, gate access card or fob, parking sticker.

**4. Do the inventory walk with the owner there.** Everything being left behind — fans, lights, geyser, wardrobes, chimney, AC units, curtain rods, the bathroom mirror — gets listed with its condition. Two ACs, one overdue a service. Geyser working, tested. Second bedroom fan makes a noise. Both of you sign or acknowledge the list; a photo of a signed page in your chat thread is fine.

**5. Confirm what has been paid and what has not.** Outstanding electricity, pending maintenance, society dues, whether the month's water tanker is settled. Get it in a message.

If the owner genuinely cannot come, do the same walk on a video call. It is less good. It is far better than nothing.

## The first week's admin

This is the boring week, and getting through it fast is the difference between settling in and camping.

**Electricity.** Find out whether the connection needs to move into your name, or stays in the owner's with you reimbursing. Both arrangements are common, and which applies depends on your state's distribution company, the owner's preference and what the agreement says. Procedures, documents and timelines vary by provider — check your own discom's website or office rather than trusting a general answer from the internet, this article included. Either way, note the consumer number and the billing cycle, and know how you will pay.

**Water.** Understand where it comes from before you need it. Corporation supply, borewell, tanker, or some combination? What time does it come, and for how long? Is there an overhead tank and a motor, and who switches the motor on — you, the watchman, or a timer? Where is the sump? In many buildings, water arrives on a schedule everybody except you already knows.

**Cooking gas.** Piped supply means a connection in your name or a transfer; a cylinder means either taking over the existing connection or arranging your own through a distributor, which is a documented process. Ask the owner what the previous tenant did — their path is usually the shortest one.

**Internet.** Order it early in week one, not late. Installation takes longer than you expect and often depends on which providers have already wired your building. Ask a neighbour who they use and whether it actually works; the honest answer is rarely on a company website.

**Society entry and gate registration.** Get into the resident system, whatever form it takes — an app, a register at the desk, a photocopy of an ID with security. Add your vehicle, and get the parking slot confirmed in writing, because parking is the most reliable source of society arguments in India. Ask about the rules for deliveries and for domestic help entry, which tend to be strict and unwritten.

**Address updates.** Bank, workplace, anything that posts you a card or a document. Do the important two or three now and the rest as they surface.

**A spare key.** Get one cut in week one and leave it somewhere sensible — a colleague, a sibling nearby, a friend across town. Not under the mat.

Keep every reference number from this week in one note. You will want them at inconvenient moments.

## What you need in week one, and what can wait

The temptation is to buy the whole home at once. Don't. Three weeks of living somewhere teaches you which corner gets morning light and where you actually eat, and both change what you buy.

| Week one — you genuinely can't function without it | Can wait a month or two |
| --- | --- |
| Bulbs and tube lights for every room | Proper light fittings and shades |
| Ceiling fans, if the flat has none | Air conditioning |
| Geyser, if it's winter or you're somewhere cold | Chimney or exhaust fan |
| A mattress, or a bed | The rest of the bedroom furniture |
| Curtains and rods — even temporary ones | Curtains you actually like |
| Gas connection and a two-burner stove | Full kitchen equipment |
| A fridge, if you cook at all | Washing machine (dhobi or laundry until then) |
| Bucket, mug, broom, mop, dustbin | Storage and organisers |
| Pressure cooker, two pans, plates, one good knife | Crockery chosen for looks |
| Power strip, extension board, a torch | Anything decorative |

Curtains matter more than new renters expect — a ground-floor flat with bare windows makes you feel watched, and you will not enjoy the place until they are up. And buy second-hand where it makes sense. Fans, wardrobes and washing machines from an outgoing tenant in the same building are a genuinely good deal, and they arrive without a delivery slot.

## Learn the building before you need it

The building runs on a system. Most of it is not written down anywhere.

**The watchman is the most useful person you will meet this month.** He knows when the water comes, which lift breaks, which plumber actually turns up, what to do when the motor trips, and when the corporation truck arrives. Introduce yourself properly on day one, learn his name, and be decent to him consistently. That is not a strategy, it is just how a building works.

**Water timing.** Ask, then verify it yourself over the first week.

**Garbage collection.** What time, which days, whether wet and dry are separated, whether it is collected at your door or at a point downstairs. Getting this wrong on day two is a poor introduction to a neighbour.

**Power backup.** Generator or inverter? Does it cover the whole flat or only some points — often fans, lights and the lift, but not the AC or the geyser. Which sockets are on it, and is there a separate charge?

**The WhatsApp group.** Nearly every building has one, and it is genuinely useful for outages, tanker news and plumber recommendations. Ask to be added. Then mute it, and read it once a day.

**Which neighbours matter.** The one directly below you, because they hear your floor. The secretary or treasurer, because they decide things. And whoever has lived there longest, because they know why everything is the way it is.

## Money habits worth forming in month one

**Pay rent traceably.** Bank transfer, UPI, cheque — anything that leaves a record with a date, an amount and a name attached. Not cash. If cash is genuinely unavoidable, get a signed receipt every single time with the month written on it. A clean trail of rent payments ends a dispute in one message instead of four weeks of argument.

**Keep the receipts.** All of them, boringly. Rent, deposit, maintenance, the move-in charge, the electrician who fixed the geyser point. You may need them for your own records at work or elsewhere — what you can and cannot claim is a question for whoever handles that for you, not for a blog.

**Make a folder.** Physical, digital, both. One place holding the signed agreement, the police verification acknowledgement if your state or society asks for one, the deposit receipt, your move-in photos and meter readings, the inventory list, utility account numbers, and every rent payment. The [rental documents checklist](/blog/rental-documents-checklist) sets out what belongs in it. Build it in week one while everything is fresh; nobody has ever reconstructed this successfully in month ten.

**Know your deposit number cold.** How much you paid, what the agreement says about deductions and notice, and by when it should come back. [Security deposits in India](/blog/security-deposits-in-india) covers what is and is not a fair deduction — read it at the start, not during the argument.

## Being the kind of tenant people want to keep

Most of getting your deposit back happens in the eleven months before you ask for it.

**Report problems in writing, and early.** A message beats a phone call because a message still exists afterwards. And early beats thorough — a slow leak reported in week two is a plumber; the same leak in month five is a damp wall and a conversation about who pays. Be specific, attach a photo, keep it friendly. "Hi, the tap in the second bathroom has started dripping, photo attached. Shall I call someone or will you arrange it?"

**Just fix the small things yourself.** A ₹40 washer, a fused bulb, a loose hinge, a slow drain that a bottle of cleaner sorts out. Calling the owner about every ₹100 problem burns goodwill you will want later for a ₹10,000 one. Anything structural, anything electrical beyond a bulb, anything to do with water pressure or the geyser — that is the owner's, and you report it.

**Noise.** Indian buildings carry sound better than anyone would like. Drilling, dragging furniture and loud music have unofficial hours in every society, and breaking them in your first fortnight becomes a reputation you keep. Planning something noisy? Tell the neighbour below first.

**Don't make permanent changes without asking.** Wall paint, a nail for a heavy shelf, an AC hole, anything drilled into tile. Ask, get a yes in writing, and you have removed a deduction argument before it exists.

**Know what you are actually owed.** Being easy to live with is not the same as being a pushover. Read up on your rights as a tenant once, calmly, while nothing is going wrong.

## The mistakes first-timers make, roughly by what they cost

1. **Not photographing the flat before moving in.** The most expensive one, because with no record of the original condition, every deduction becomes your word against theirs. Forty minutes of work.
2. **Signing without reading — especially notice period, lock-in and deduction clauses.** A lock-in you did not notice gets expensive the day your job moves cities.
3. **Paying cash with no receipt.** Both the deposit and the monthly rent. Untraceable money is unrecoverable money.
4. **Budgeting for rent and not for setup.** Fans, lights, geyser and curtains all arrive in the same month as the deposit, and that month is the tightest of the year.
5. **Not taking meter readings on day one.** You inherit somebody else's bill with no way to prove you should not have.
6. **Letting a small repair run.** Cheap in week two. Contested in month six.
7. **Buying furniture in the first week.** You do not know the flat yet.
8. **Never learning the water schedule.** Not expensive. Just miserable, once.

## Looking ahead: renewal, or leaving

Around month nine, two questions arrive, and both are better thought about before they are urgent.

**Renewal.** Most agreements run eleven months and many carry an agreed increase. Look at yours now so the number is not a surprise. If you have been a good tenant, say so when it comes up — a reliable payer who does not call at midnight has real value to an owner, and that is leverage worth using politely.

**Leaving.** Give notice exactly as the agreement requires, in writing, and keep the acknowledgement. Clean properly, arrange your own repairs rather than having them deducted at the owner's price, and take a full set of photos on the way out — the mirror image of the ones from day one. Take final meter readings together, and agree the deposit return in writing before you hand back the keys.

A first tenancy that ends cleanly is also a reference, and you will want one for the next place.

## Where StayOnMap fits

Very little of the above is something a website can do for you. Nobody can read your agreement or count your bulbs.

Two things we did build for exactly this reader. Every listing has to state rent, deposit and maintenance — they are required fields, so an owner cannot post without them — which means you see the real monthly number before you spend a Saturday travelling to something you cannot afford. And there is no brokerage, the cost first-timers are least prepared for; you contact the owner directly.

The homepage is a map rather than a list, which matters more than it sounds when you do not know a city yet. You can see what is genuinely around a place instead of trusting an area name in a headline. [Why maps beat lists](/blog/why-maps-beat-lists-for-finding-a-home) makes that case at length.

---

If you are reading this a week before you get keys: photograph the empty flat, read the meters, count the keys, buy bulbs. Everything else can be worked out over a weekend. And if you are reading it on the floor of an empty room with your phone torch propped against the wall — that part is normal, and it gets sorted by Tuesday.

For the whole picture, from search to signature, start with the [complete guide to renting in India](/blog/complete-guide-to-renting-in-india).
